The graph and agent subjects prepare the Year 2 transverse projects [Y2.1](../../projects/index.html#y2-1) (graph-based question answering), [Y2.2](../../projects/index.html#y2-2) (verifiable rewards) and [Y2.4](../../projects/index.html#y2-4) (agent reliability).

### Solo projects {#projects-solo}

1.  **[Solo · ≈ 20 h] An honest leaderboard: contamination and judge calibration.** Question: how much of a benchmark score survives a contamination check, and how far can an LLM judge be trusted? Chapters used: ch. 1, 2.
    -   Implement a reusable harness: the 13-gram overlap detector of ch. 1 run against a public pre-training sample (a shard of Dolma, Soldaini et al., 2024), and 20 or more regenerated variants of GSM8K items (Cobbe et al., 2021) with new numbers and names. Report each score as the raw / variant / overlap triple of Proposition 1.2.
    -   Calibrate an open LLM judge on the 3.3k expert votes of the MT-Bench human judgments (Zheng et al., 2023), in both answer orders; measure agreement, the position-flip rate and a verbosity bias (pad correct answers).
    -   Models: two or three open instruction models of 1–8B parameters, on a free GPU tier.
    -   Deliverables: code, a 4–6 page report, a 10-minute talk. Success: every score given with a 95% interval and its variant gap; the judge's agreement with humans, with an interval, set against the 81% human–human level (ties excluded).

2.  **[Solo · ≈ 20 h] Paper study: speculative decoding meets 4-bit quantization (Leviathan, Kalman and Matias, 2023).** Question: does Theorem 7.2 predict the measured speedup, and what does quantizing the target cost in acceptance and quality? Chapters used: ch. 7, 1.
    -   Implement speculative sampling with residual resampling (Definition 7.1) for a pair that shares a tokenizer, such as Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct as draft and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct as target, on a free T4 GPU.
    -   Measure the acceptance rate per domain — prose (WikiText-103), code (HumanEval prompts), math (GSM8K) — the tokens per target pass, and the best draft length from the speedup formula of exam question 2.
    -   Quantize the target with GPTQ and with AWQ (7.2). Re-measure acceptance, latency, memory, GSM8K accuracy and the refusal rate on 100 AdvBench prompts (Zou et al., 2023), not only perplexity.
    -   Deliverables: code, a 4–6 page report, a 10-minute talk. Success: measured tokens per pass within 10% of the theorem at the measured acceptance rate, or the gap explained (acceptances are correlated); a speed–memory–quality table with intervals.

### Group projects {#projects-group}

1.  **[Group of 4 · ≈ 30 h each] Paper study: serialize, retrieve or encode? A KG-QA bake-off around G-Retriever (He et al., 2024).** Question: under a fixed token budget, when does a structural component beat serialization or long context — the open question of ch. 8? The subject connects this module to [Graph ML ch. 10](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch10) and [Advanced GNN 8.3](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html#ch8), and is a light version of Y2.1. Chapters used: ch. 3, 4, 8.
    -   Data: the WebQSP and SceneGraphs splits released with G-Retriever; one open LLM of 1–8B parameters for all systems.
    -   Member 1: serialization — Talk-like-a-Graph encodings of the 2-hop subgraph (Proposition 8.1), and a long-context baseline that stuffs the graph up to the budget (ch. 3).
    -   Member 2: GraphRAG — Leiden communities, their summaries, local and global search (ch. 4; Graph ML 10.1).
    -   Member 3: a light G-Retriever — PCST or shortest-path subgraph, a GNN and one graph token, frozen LLM (Definition 8.2).
    -   Member 4: the harness — Hit@1, a hallucination rate (answers naming entities absent from the graph), tokens and cost per query, an LLM judge calibrated as in ch. 1.
    -   Deliverables: code, a 6–8 page report, a 15-minute talk. Success: the four systems at the same budget, Hit@1 with intervals per question type, and a reasoned answer to the open question of ch. 8 for these data.

2.  **[Group of 3 · ≈ 30 h each] Does RLVR teach graph algorithms or just select them?** Question: the "select or create" debate of ch. 2, on the master's own domain. The subject connects this module to [LLMs ch. 5](../m2-large-language-models/index.html#ch5) (GRPO) and [Reinforcement Learning ch. 5](../m1p2-reinforcement-learning/index.html#ch5). Chapters used: ch. 2, 8.
    -   Tasks: NLGraph-style connectivity, shortest path and topological sort on random NetworkX graphs, with rewards checked exactly by NetworkX (Definition 2.2). Train on 5–15 nodes; test on 20–40 nodes and on an unseen encoding (Proposition 8.1).
    -   Member 1: mini-GRPO with LoRA on Qwen2.5-0.5B- or 1.5B-Instruct (TRL library), logging accuracy and generation length (2.3).
    -   Member 2: the distillation baseline — supervised fine-tuning on verifier-filtered traces of a larger open model, at equal compute.
    -   Member 3: the test of Yue et al. (2025) — pass@k of the base and trained models for k up to 256. If RLVR only selects, the base model catches up at large k.
    -   Deliverables: code, a 6–8 page report, a 15-minute talk. Success: in- and out-of-distribution accuracy with intervals for the base, RLVR and distilled models, and pass@k curves that decide between the two readings on this domain.

3.  **[Group of 4 · ≈ 30 h each] A long-lived agent with structured memory.** Question: which memory design keeps an agent reliable over many sessions, and at what token cost? The subject uses the tracing of [ML Ops ch. 8](../m2-mlops-llm-engineering/index.html#ch8). Chapters used: ch. 3, 4, 9.
    -   Data: the very long conversations of LoCoMo and their questions (Maharana et al., 2024), plus a multi-session task of the group's choice (research assistant or support desk) with three or more tools.
    -   Members 1–3: one memory each — a plain vector store; a Generative-Agents memory stream with reflection (Proposition 4.1); MemGPT-style paging or an entity-graph memory.
    -   Member 4: the ReAct agent and the harness — per-step success, the chain law of Proposition 9.2, and the single- versus multi-agent ablation at equal token budget.
    -   Deliverables: code, a 6–8 page report, a 15-minute talk. Success: LoCoMo accuracy per question category and tokens per answer for each memory, with intervals; measured task success set against the prediction of Proposition 9.2 from the measured per-step success.

### Written exam (proposal) {#projects-exam}

Format: 2 hours, one handwritten A4 sheet allowed, a non-programmable calculator, four questions. The fiche displays no exam, so this is a mock.

1.  **Question (5 points).** (a) What does a contaminated benchmark score estimate, and which three numbers should a paper report instead of one? (b) Why is the KV cache of a transformer a *feature* and not only a cost, compared with the state of Mamba or RWKV? (c) Li et al. (2024) find that long context beats RAG on average. Why is RAG still deployed, and what does Self-Route do?

    *Expected*: (a) a mixture of memory and generalization, so the estimand shifts (Proposition 1.2); report the raw score, the score on regenerated variants and an overlap measure, and read the gap as an interval. (b) The cache stores every past key and value exactly, so any token can be recalled precisely; an SSM or RWKV compresses the history into a fixed-size state and fails exact recall, hence hybrids such as Jamba (6.3).

    (c) Cost: RAG sends a few excerpts. Self-Route asks the model whether the excerpts suffice and sends the full context only when they do not: comparable quality for 39% to 65% less cost (3.4).

2.  **Question (6 points).** A draft model's tokens are accepted with probability 0.8 each. (a) With a draft length of 4, compute the expected number of tokens per target pass (Theorem 7.2). (b) One draft step costs 0.1 target step, so an iteration with draft length $\gamma$ costs $0.1\gamma + 1$. Compute the speedup for draft lengths 2, 4, 6 and 7, and give the best one. (c) Two models are 0.5 points apart on a 500-question benchmark. Give the 95% Hoeffding half-width of each accuracy and conclude.

    *Expected*: (a) $(1 - 0.8^5)/0.2 = 3.36$ tokens. (b) The speedup is the expected number of tokens divided by the iteration cost:
    $$\frac{2.44}{1.2} = 2.03, \quad \frac{3.36}{1.4} = 2.40, \quad \frac{3.95}{1.6} = 2.47, \quad \frac{4.16}{1.7} = 2.45,$$
    so the best draft length is 6, and the curve is flat between 5 and 7.

    (c) By Theorem 0.3 of [Machine Learning](../m1p1-machine-learning/index.html#ch0), the half-width is
    $$\sqrt{\frac{\ln(2/0.05)}{2 \cdot 500}} \approx 0.061,$$
    about 6 points, twelve times the gap: the ranking says nothing.

3.  **Question (5 points).** For the Switch loss of Proposition 5.2: (a) with four experts, $f = (0.7, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1)$ and $P = (0.6, 0.2, 0.1, 0.1)$, compute the loss divided by its weight, and compare with uniform routing. (b) Prove that the loss is at least its weight when the loads and the router masses are similarly ordered. (c) Redo (a) with two experts, $f = (0.9, 0.1)$ and $P = (0.45, 0.55)$. What does the result say about the loss?

    *Expected*: (a) the sum of the products is $0.42 + 0.02 + 0.01 + 0.01 = 0.46$, so the ratio is $4 \times 0.46 = 1.84$, above the value 1 of uniform routing. (b) Chebyshev's sum inequality, as in the proof of Proposition 5.2: the average of the products is at least the product of the averages, which is the square of the inverse number of experts.

    (c) The sum is $0.405 + 0.055 = 0.46$ and the ratio $2 \times 0.46 = 0.92 < 1$: an anti-monotone pair goes below the "minimum". The bound needs co-monotone sequences; the loss is a load proxy, whose gradient (equal to the load) still pushes the loaded experts down.

4.  **Question (4 points).** In ring attention (Proposition 3.4), a device receives the key/value blocks one at a time and updates its running maximum, normalizer and output. Prove by induction that after the last block, the output divided by the normalizer is the exact softmax attention over the whole sequence. Why multiply by $e^{m - m'}$ at each update?

    *Expected*: invariant after the blocks seen so far: $m$ is their largest score, $\ell = \sum e^{s - m}$ and $O = \sum e^{s - m} v$. It holds at the start (empty sums, $m = -\infty$). At an update the old sums are moved to the new reference by the factor $e^{m - m'}$ and the new block adds its terms.

    At the end the common factor $e^{-m}$ cancels in $O/\ell$, leaving the softmax-weighted average of the values. The rescaling keeps every exponent at most 0 (no overflow) and puts old and new terms on one reference.

### Grading rubric (proposal) {#projects-rubric}

The rubric grades the continuous part (portfolio and project); the written exam, if an instructor uses it, is graded on its own.

| Criterion | Weight | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Reading-note portfolio (Ex. 1) | 20 % | one sheet per session with claim, evidence, costs, reproducibility and LLGA link; two sheets in depth |
| Question and protocol | 15 % | a falsifiable question, named baselines, a fixed budget and a contamination check stated before the runs |
| Implementation and reproducibility | 20 % | code that runs from a clean clone, fixed seeds, logged costs (tokens, GPU-hours) and versions |
| Results and critical analysis | 30 % | intervals rather than points, ablations, failure cases, and the reading grid of ch. 0 applied to one's own claims |
| Report and talk | 15 % | a 4–8 page report a peer can check, and a 10–15 minute talk defended at the board |
